opening_message: There's a big woody vine climbing up a tree at the edge of my yard and I want to know what it actually is before I do anything with it. No leaves on it right now, dead of winter. What do you think it is?

slots.name: leaf_persistence_season
slots.value: No, no leaves on it at all right now, it's completely bare -- I think it drops them for winter.
slots.description: Confirms a deciduous, dormant vine; on its own this doesn't distinguish American from Chinese wisteria.

slots.name: bloom_timing
slots.value: It hasn't bloomed yet this year, it's the middle of winter -- and honestly I don't remember exactly whether the flowers showed up before or after the leaves came out last spring.
slots.description: The single most decisive diagnostic (blooms before/as leaves emerge = Chinese wisteria; blooms after leaves emerge but before fully developed = American wisteria, per data/ground_truth/wisteria-frutescens.yaml) is unavailable this season and wasn't reliably observed last year either -- this is the crux of why remote identification isn't achievable here.

slots.name: seed_pod_texture
slots.value: I don't see any old seed pods hanging on it anywhere, must not have had any last year, or they've since fallen off.
slots.description: The other decisive diagnostic (smooth pod texture = American wisteria; velvety pod texture = Chinese wisteria, per the same ground-truth file) is also unavailable -- no pods to inspect.

slots.name: vine_thickness
slots.value: Pretty thick and woody at the base, it's clearly been climbing that tree a long while.
slots.description: Doesn't distinguish the two wisteria species; just indicates an established vine, which both species can become.

slots.name: leaflet_count_recalled
slots.value: Hard to say for sure with no leaves right now, but I remember it having a bunch of little leaflets in a row along each stem last summer.
slots.description: Compound pinnate leaves are shared by both wisteria species, so a general leaflet description doesn't discriminate between them even when recalled accurately.

ecological_framing_notes: If this vine is confirmed as American wisteria (Wisteria frutescens), it is a native species with fragrant flowers valuable to pollinators and no invasive spread risk, and a correct answer should say so once (or if) identity is actually confirmed. But for this specific card, both decisive field marks are unavailable, so a response that confidently asserts either the native-and-beneficial framing or the invasive-and-remove framing without flagging that genuine uncertainty is not naming the right thing -- the correct answer here is the referral itself (a photo to the county Cooperative Extension office, or waiting for bloom/pod season), which the Q6 judge should not penalize as 'no ecological framing' when the reason is exactly this appropriate caution.
referral_reason: both of the field marks that reliably separate Chinese wisteria (invasive) from American wisteria (native) -- seed pod texture and bloom timing relative to leaf-out -- are unavailable here: the vine is dormant with no leaves, hasn't bloomed yet this season, and has no old seed pods to inspect. Per the same ground truth this corpus already cites (data/ground_truth/wisteria-frutescens.yaml), when a homeowner can't check either test the correct next step is a photo submitted to their county Cooperative Extension office for a positive identification, not a guess
